To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) team membership is not static and is subject to change in response to changing team demands, and (2) team dynamics include within-team subgroup dynamics that are not only common, but also functional in terms of facilitating team effectiveness.
management teams are not static but rather adaptive, self-adjusted teams that interact at different levels of analysis.
the composition of management teams is dynamic and adaptive and that management teams are self-adjusting, self-regulating, self-optimizing, and self-organizing systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the team phenomenon, and how the concept of a team may be better conceptualised in future research.
how management teams are conceptualised, modelled, and studied.
the nature, functioning and effectiveness of management teams.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a management team is a self-regulating group of individuals who share a common identity, purpose and task interdependence, and who interact with each other at multiple levels of the organisation to adapt to and respond to changing task demands and environmental conditions.
the management team is an adaptive, self-adjustment team that interacts at multiple levels of analyses.
management teams are self-adjusting teams.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated the importance of a dynamic, self-regulating perspective on the nature of management teams.
management teams are self-adjusting, adaptive units of analysis that interact at multiple organisational levels.
management teams are adaptive, self-adjustment systems that interact at multiple, nested levels of analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of management teams should be broadened and deepened.
management teams are not static and that they are not necessarily indivisible units of study.
future research needs to be more sensitive to the dynamic, interactive, self-adjusting functioning of teams, including their spontaneous, informal subgroups.
